title: Pasta e patate
subtitle: Neapolitan pasta and potato soup
excerpt: A thick, starchy, deeply comforting Neapolitan soup in which potatoes and pasta cook together until the potato breaks down into the broth, thickening it. Often called the 'soup of the poor', it is one of Naples' great dishes.
sourceNotes: Pasta e patate is a canonical Neapolitan dish documented in Eduardo De Filippo's writings and in Ada Boni's Il Talismano della Felicità (1929). It also appears in Jeanne Carola Francesconi's La Cucina Napoletana (1965), the authoritative reference on Neapolitan cooking. The soup is associated with cucina povera and has been a staple of the Neapolitan table for at least two centuries.

recipe.freezeNotes: Not suitable for freezing: the pasta overcooks on reheating and the potatoes lose their texture.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made and served the same day. The soup thickens considerably as it stands; add more stock or water when reheating.

content.text: Pasta e patate is not a soup with pasta in it; it is something denser and more substantial. The potatoes cook until they partially break down, thickening the broth with their starch. The pasta finishes cooking in this thick liquid and absorbs it. The result sits at the boundary between a soup and a stew. Neapolitans eat it in this thick state, calling it 'azzeccato' (stuck together); others prefer to add more stock and serve it slightly looser. Both are right.

items.prepNote: waxy variety, peeled and cut into 1 cm dice
mixed short pasta shapes: tubetti, ditalini, mezzani broken into pieces. Or one shape alone
rind, added to the soup; plus grated, to serve

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, and garlic and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until they have darkened and slightly reduced. Add the potato and stir to coat.
Pour in the stock. If using a Parmesan rind, add it now. Bring to the boil and simmer for 20 minutes until the potatoes are just tender. Remove the Parmesan rind if using.

Roughly crush about a quarter of the potato pieces with the back of a spoon to thicken the broth. Add the pasta and cook for the time given on the packet, stirring frequently as the soup thickens and the pasta tends to stick. Season well.
Serve in deep bowls with a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil, scattered with basil or parsley, and grated Parmesan on the side.

items.symptom: Pasta is glued to the bottom of the pan
items.cause: Too little liquid or heat too high as the pasta finishes cooking
items.fix: Stir frequently in the last stage. If it catches, add a splash of stock or water and reduce the heat.

content.text: Pasta e patate is an invention of Naples and the Campanian hinterland. The cooking of the poor combined the two cheapest starches (pasta and potato) into a single dish that was filling, cheap, and deeply satisfying. The Neapolitan playwright Eduardo De Filippo wrote about it with the same affection he gave his best characters. It is the kind of dish that improves with age. The pasta thickens the remaining soup as it stands. The next-day leftovers, eaten cold or just reheated, have a sticky, nearly porridge-like quality that the Neapolitans find entirely irresistible.
